deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a page of German lecture or reading notes on ancient history, written in Gauss's student hand. It belongs to the same sequence as the previous page (Seleucid Syria) and the next page (Ptolemaic Egypt). The style and section numbering suggest notes on a course such as Heeren's at Göttingen; that attribution is a guess, not established. The page has two parts.

(1) End of the Seleucid section. The first line finishes a sentence from p.166, roughly '...Cleopatra, welche Antiochus Sidetes [heirathete?] ... hinrichten'.
- Tryphon dies in 138 BC.
- Antiochus (VII Sidetes) secures the throne.
- In 132 he campaigns against the Parthians and dies on the campaign.
- Meanwhile his brother (Demetrius II) escapes captivity and becomes king again in 128.
- A rival, Alexander Zebinas (Zabinas), rises against him; Demetrius is killed in 126.
- In 125 Cleopatra (Thea) murders her eldest son (Seleucus V) and defeats Alexander Zebinas.
- Antiochus Grypus (VIII) reigns beside her and murders her in 122.
- Some years later Grypus fights his half-brother Antiochus of Cyzicus (IX Cyzicenus).
- In 85 Tigranes, king of Armenia, holds Syria; in 65 it becomes a Roman province.

(2) Heading '2) Geschichte des Aegyptischen Reichs unter den Ptolemaeern 323–30 a. c.' (ante Christum). Description of Alexandria:
- It lies between Lake Mareotis and the Canopic mouth of the Nile.
- A canal runs from the Nile to the lake, and there is a harbour on the lake.
- The city is divided into 4 quarters, the finest being the Bruchium.

There are no derivations or computations to reconstruct.
errors: Not a mathematical page, so there are no mathematical errors. Several historical dates are approximate or slightly off by modern chronology.
Antiochus VII's Parthian campaign began c. 131/130 BC, and he died in 129, not 132.
Demetrius II regained the throne in 129, not 128.
Demetrius II died in 125 (near Tyre), not 126.
Cleopatra Thea's death is usually dated c. 121/120, not 122.
Tigranes' control of Syria is usually dated 83 BC, not 85.
Pompey made Syria a province in 64/63 BC, not 65.

Ancient sources (e.g. Philo) usually describe five lettered districts of Alexandria. The 'four quarters' is the lecturer's or the note-taker's simplification. These discrepancies probably reflect the lecture source of c. 1790s rather than Gauss's own error.

results.what: Historical lecture notes on late Seleucid dynasty and on the topography of Ptolemaic Alexandria
results.usually_credited_to: Standard content of late-18th-century Göttingen ancient-history teaching (e.g. A. H. L. Heeren); the source is unsure

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical note-taking with no mathematical content. That Gauss attended or read history lectures as a student is unremarkable.

checkable.asserts: The Ptolemaic period as given (323–30 BC) spans 293 years.
The interval from Tryphon's death (138) to Demetrius II's restoration (128) as given in the notes is 10 years. This matches the '10 Jahr' captivity stated on p.166, counted from 138.

transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'Herzogs[?]' is doubtful. It is the end of the sentence begun on p.166 about Cleopatra and Antiochus Sidetes. The reading is unclear; possibly a verb such as 'heirathete' or a name followed by 'hinrichten'.
Line 2: 'das Erbe[?]' may instead read 'das Reich'.
Line 3: 'Parter' is correctly transcribed as written (i.e. Parther).
'Tygranis' is as written; it means Tigranes.
'hatte[?] dieser einen Krieg' is plausible; '85 hatte[?] Tygranis' may read '85 bekam/hatte'.
